name: Gabapentin
route_note: Oral capsules, tablets and solution, usually three times daily; once-daily and prodrug extended-release forms.

discovery.note: Designed in the 1970s as a lipophilic, brain-penetrant analogue of GABA; it was later found not to act on GABA receptors.

rx_status: prescription; controlled (UK Class C, Schedule V in some US states)
tagline: Gabapentinoid used for neuropathic pain and focal seizures
summary: Gabapentin is a GABA analogue that binds the alpha-2-delta subunit of voltage-gated calcium channels. Approved for focal seizures and postherpetic neuralgia, it is very widely prescribed for neuropathic pain, and misuse concerns have led to controls in several countries.
mechanism: Despite its design as a GABA analogue, gabapentin does not bind GABA receptors. It binds the alpha-2-delta-1 subunit of presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels, reducing their trafficking to the membrane and decreasing release of excitatory neurotransmitters such as glutamate and substance P.
This dampens hyperexcitability in sensitised pain pathways and in seizure-prone cortex. Absorption depends on a saturable L-amino acid transporter, so bioavailability falls at higher doses.
uses: Focal seizures with or without secondary generalisation (adjunct and monotherapy)

history.title: US approval
history.detail: The FDA approves Neurontin as adjunctive therapy for partial seizures.

history.title: Postherpetic neuralgia
history.detail: The FDA approves gabapentin for postherpetic neuralgia.

history.title: Off-label marketing settlement
history.detail: Pfizer's Warner-Lambert unit pleads guilty and pays $430 million over illegal promotion of Neurontin for unapproved uses.

history.title: Generics
history.detail: Generic gabapentin launches in the US.

history.title: New formulations
history.detail: Gralise and the prodrug gabapentin enacarbil (Horizant) are approved in the US.

history.title: Controls and warnings
history.detail: The UK reclassifies gabapentin and pregabalin as Class C controlled drugs; the FDA warns of serious breathing problems when combined with opioids or in respiratory disease.

pk.bioavailability: dose-dependent: about 60% at low doses, falling at higher doses (saturable transport)
pk.excretion: renal, unchanged; dose reduced in renal impairment

serious: Respiratory depression with opioids or other CNS depressants

facts: Gabapentin is among the most prescribed drugs in the US, with much of its use off-label for pain.
Internal documents released in the Neurontin litigation became a landmark case study of off-label drug promotion.
